entry.title: AI Governance and Cost Monitoring with SAP AI Agent Hub and SAP for Me
entry.content:
Executive Summary

As organisations deploy hundreds or even thousands of AI agents across SAP and non-SAP environments, governance becomes a critical architectural concern. Before agent ecosystems scale beyond operational control, Enterprise Architects must establish visibility, policy enforcement, observability, identity management, and cost controls.

SAP addresses this challenge through two complementary capabilities:

  • SAP AI Agent Hub provides discovery, inventory, governance, observability, verification, and lifecycle management for AI agents, large language models (LLMs), and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers across heterogeneous landscapes.
  • SAP for Me acts as the operational and activation layer through which SAP-managed AI capabilities and autonomous services are provisioned, consumed, and tracked within the SAP ecosystem.

Together, they form the foundation for enterprise-scale AI governance – pairing architectural oversight with real-time cost transparency.

Why AI Agent Governance Is Now an Architecture Problem

Every enterprise that has moved beyond AI pilots is hitting the same wall: agent sprawl. Departments are deploying AI agents from SAP, Microsoft, Google, AWS, and custom-built solutions often without central oversight. The questions pile up fast: Which agents are running in production? Who owns them? What data can they access? How much are they costing us? Are they compliant with the EU AI Act?

SAP rightly frames this as a board-level issue: as agents shift from augmenting decisions to executing autonomous processes, the governance gap becomes an operational and regulatory risk.

SAP News: Agent Sprawl – Why AI Governance Is Now a Board-Level Issue

For Enterprise Architects this is familiar territory, it mirrors the application sprawl we have managed for years but with far higher velocity and non-deterministic behaviour. Agents execute processes, call APIs, access data, and make decisions, yet organisations quickly lose sight of which exist, who owns them, and what they cost. SAP calls this the AI equivalent of Shadow IT: Shadow AI. SAP addresses it with two complementary capabilities: one for governance and one for cost – explored below.

The Enterprise Architect's Mandate

EAs sit at the intersection of business strategy, technology standards, and compliance – exactly where agent governance decisions belong. For agentic AI, that mandate expands to four areas:

  • Agent estate management: a curated inventory of all agents, LLMs, and MCP servers, mapped to business capabilities and owners.
  • Architecture standards and guardrails: reference architectures, identity models, and policy frameworks for deployment.
  • Governance mechanism design: the right level of human oversight (Human-in-Command, Human-in-the-Loop, Human-on-the-Loop, or Autonomous) per use case, based on risk.
  • Cost stewardship: ensuring AI investments deliver measurable outcomes rather than quietly consuming budget through unmonitored token sprawl.

SAP AI Agent Hub: The Governance Command Centre

SAP AI Agent Hub is a vendor-agnostic command centre, a single entry point for the discovery and governance of AI agents, LLMs, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers across the landscape. Built on SAP LeanIX Application Portfolio Management, it brings enterprise architecture context – applications, capabilities, and organisational structures directly into the governance workflow.

Crucially, the AI Agent Hub is not limited to SAP. It governs agents from Microsoft, Google, AWS, Databricks, ServiceNow, and custom builds, and leverages open standards – A2A (Agent-to-Agent) for multi-agent collaboration and MCP for standardised tool connectivity. It reached General Availability in November 2025 as part of SAP LeanIX Application Portfolio Management and is available at no additional charge for SAP LeanIX customers.

SAP for Me: The Operational Cost Lens

While the Hub provides governance-level visibility, SAP for Me is where customers activate AI features and track consumption in near real-time. Within SAP's agentic architecture, an EA can register an agent in the Hub, apply governance assessments, validate identity, approve policies, and trigger provisioning through SAP for Me – a governed onboarding path rather than uncontrolled deployment. In short: the Hub is the control tower; SAP for Me is the operational service portal.

The Finance & Legal area of SAP for Me includes a dedicated Business AI tab showing AI Units available (current monthly balance), consumption by feature (including autonomous agent actions), expiration tracking (the 12-month window), and overage monitoring (pay-per-use charges once the balance is exhausted). This is the commercial truth that underpins FinOps decisions and combined with the Hub's architectural context, EAs can correlate cost to value at the agent level.

For custom agents, SAP AI Core provides usage-based infrastructure for AI model management. Custom predictive models incur compute, storage, and hourly baseline charges; foundation models with grounding instead accrue token-based charges. Detailed consumption is available in the SAP BTP cockpit under the customer's global account.

The Observability Stack

Effective governance needs multi-layer observability. SAP's stack combines four components, each with a distinct purpose:

  • Layer 1 – SAP AI Agent Hub: governance-level visibility – session health, goal-completion rates, tool-call correctness, and root-cause analysis.
  • Layer 2 – SAP Cloud ALM: operational monitoring with agent dashboards, evaluation rates, error causes, and performance trends via OpenTelemetry.
  • Layer 3 – SAP Signavio Process Intelligence: behavioural analysis and agent-execution mining – process conformance, cost per execution, and impact on KPIs such as cycle time and throughput.
  • Layer 4 – SAP Cloud Logging: technical telemetry on OpenSearch – logs, metrics, and traces for LLM-based applications.

Recommendations for Enterprise Architects

  • Establish a governed registry from day one. Stand up the Hub as your system of record even for your first production agent – retroactive governance is far more expensive.
  • Treat agents as first-class architecture assets. Give each a named owner, a mapped capability, a risk classification, and a place in your architecture reviews.
  • Apply tiered oversight. Use the four-level autonomy model and assign oversight based on risk, not fear.
  • Operationalise FinOps for AI. Combine SAP for Me consumption data, SAP AI Core technical costs, and chargeback models; set budget alerts early.
  • Build observability by maturity. Start with the Hub plus SAP for Me, add SAP Cloud ALM, then layer in SAP Signavio as the estate scales.
  • Leverage open standards. Adopt A2A and MCP to avoid lock-in at the orchestration layer.

Conclusion

The shift from AI assistants to autonomous agents is architectural, not incremental. Governing agents demands the same discipline we apply to application portfolios and security architectures. SAP AI Agent Hub provides the governance command centre; SAP for Me provides the operational cost lens. Together they form the foundation for responsible, scalable AI adoption. As Enterprise Architects, we are the curators of enterprise context and the designers of governance mechanisms. The agents are arriving – the only question is whether governance arrives with them, or after the damage is done.

entry.title: Beyond Architecture: Through My Lens on the Multidimensional Architect in the Age of AI
entry.content:
The Beginning – 2024: Rethinking the Role of an Enterprise Architect

My journey with the SAP Multidimensional Architect Program began in 2024, when I had the opportunity to attend its inaugural program. What made the experience particularly impactful was that it challenged my traditional understanding of Enterprise Architecture and broadened my perspective on what it truly takes to become an effective Enterprise Architect.

Building on the foundation established in 2024, the 2025 edition of the SAP Multidimensional Architect Program took the Enterprise Architect journey a step further. While the first year challenged us to rethink the role of an architect and develop the right mindset, 2025 focused on expanding our capabilities and becoming truly multidimensional  bringing together technology expertise, business acumen, strategic thinking, leadership, and the ability to influence people and organizations.

2025 – Becoming a Multidimensional Architect: Beyond Technology, Towards Business Impact

The SAP Multidimensional Architect Program 2025 was a transformative five-day journey that brought together technology, business strategy, AI, leadership, and human connections. It challenged traditional perceptions of Enterprise Architecture and reinforced that the future architect must be more than a technology expert  someone who can connect business vision with technology execution, embrace AI-driven innovation, influence organizational change, and inspire people through collaboration and purpose.

One of the strongest messages was that architecture must start with business outcomes, not technology choices. Architects need to understand the business context, recognize organizational challenges, translate strategic objectives into technology-enabled capabilities, and help decision-makers see the value of the transformation journey. It is not enough to recommend a solution; we must be able to explain why it matters, what value it creates, and how it moves the organization closer to its long-term vision.

The program also reinforced several dimensions that define the modern Enterprise Architect:

  • Business and strategic thinking: Move beyond solution design to understand business priorities, operating models, value drivers, and the broader transformation agenda.

  • AI and emerging technologies: Develop the curiosity and understanding to explore AI-driven innovation, assess its potential, and identify meaningful opportunities to create business value.

  • Leadership and influence: Architecture is increasingly about influencing decisions, aligning stakeholders, navigating complexity, and bringing people together around a shared vision even without direct authority.

  • Communication and storytelling: A compelling architecture vision needs a compelling story. Architects must simplify complexity, communicate with different audiences, articulate the value of change, and build confidence in the roadmap.

  • Human-centered architecture: Technology transformation is ultimately about people. Empathy, active listening, collaboration, trust, and the ability to inspire change are as important as technical depth.

  • Collaboration and community: Learning from peers, exchanging experiences, challenging assumptions, and building professional relationships strengthen the collective capabilities of the Enterprise Architecture community.

Perhaps the biggest takeaway was that Enterprise Architecture is not just about designing systems, frameworks, or roadmaps; it is about building capabilities, enabling decisions, connecting people, and creating sustainable business outcomes. The program concluded not simply with the completion of five days of learning, but with the beginning of a stronger, more connected, and collaborative Enterprise Architect community.

My reflections and personal takeaways

For me, the 2025 program reinforced an important shift in how I approach my own professional journey: moving from being a technology leader who delivers complex transformations to becoming an architect who shapes transformation strategy and business outcomes.

With more than two decades of experience in the SAP ecosystem, working across large-scale transformations, S/4HANA conversions via Downtime Optimized Conversion (DoC) , Zero Downtime Option (ZDO), and complex customer landscapes, I have seen firsthand that technical excellence is essential  but it is only one part of the equation. The ability to connect technology decisions with business priorities, communicate the bigger picture, influence stakeholders, and lead people through change is what creates lasting impact.

The overall program experience and listening to all the intellectual leaders inspired me to look beyond the technical boundaries of Enterprise Architecture and reflect on how knowledge, experience, and practical insights can be transformed into something meaningful for the wider SAP community. It motivated me to bring together my years of hands-on experience in S/4HANA transformations and Zero Downtime Option (ZDO) into my book, “Mastering S/4HANA Upgrades and Updates via ZDO – Zero Downtime Optimization.” Writing this book became an opportunity to share practical learnings, address real-world upgrade and downtime challenges, and help fellow architects and SAP professionals navigate complex transformation journeys with greater confidence.

If 2024 was about changing the architect's mindset, 2025 was about expanding those dimensions  and turning experience into knowledge that can inspire and empower others. The program reinforced that architects should not only design and deliver transformation but also contribute to the community, share their expertise, and create lasting value beyond individual projects. It also set the stage for the next evolution in 2026: How do we architect for an AI-driven and increasingly autonomous enterprise?

2026 – Architecting the Autonomous Enterprise: The Enterprise Architect in the Age of AI

If 2024 was about changing the architect's mindset and 2025 was about expanding the architect's dimensions, 2026 brought us to the next frontier: redefining Enterprise Architecture in the age of AI and the Autonomous Enterprise.

The 2026 SAP Multidimensional Architect Program, hosted at the SAP Institute for Product and Engineering in San Ramon, brought together more than 100 architects for another immersive learning experience. The conversations moved beyond understanding emerging technologies to exploring how AI, agentic capabilities, trusted enterprise data, strategic leadership, and human intelligence will shape the future of organizations  and, more importantly, the future role of Enterprise Architects.

What stood out was the shift from discussing what AI can do to understanding how architects can help organizations adopt it responsibly, connect it to business priorities, and translate its potential into measurable outcomes.

The Future-Ready Architect: Learn, Unlearn and Relearn

The initial program sessions set the tone by exploring the Future-Ready Architect, the Autonomous Enterprise, AI-enabled productivity, and the human skills required to navigate continuous change.

One of the strongest messages was the importance of moving from IQ to EQ to LQ – Learning Quotient. In a world where technology and AI capabilities are evolving rapidly, technical knowledge alone is not enough. Our ability to remain curious, challenge assumptions, adapt, and continuously learn will determine how effectively we lead through change.

Some important takeaways are - 

  • Learn, unlearn and relearn: Be willing to challenge established practices and continuously evolve our thinking.

  • Balance technology with human intelligence: Combine technical expertise with emotional intelligence, empathy, and sound human judgment.

  • Connect architecture to business outcomes: Ensure technology and AI initiatives solve meaningful business problems.

  • Practice the art of subtraction: Simplify complexity, eliminate unnecessary work, and create space to focus on what truly matters.

  • Build responsible AI strategies: Treat governance, accountability, and trust as essential elements of AI adoption.

The message was clear: the future-ready architect is not necessarily the person who knows the most technologies, but the one who can adapt, ask better questions, and bring the right people and capabilities together.

 From Technology Advisor to Strategic Business Leader

Program moved with more deep dive focus sessions into how AI is changing the enterprise and the role architects must play in shaping that change. The discussions connected the Autonomous Enterprise, industry AI, trusted data and context with the evolving strategic responsibilities of Enterprise Architecture.

A particularly powerful metaphor was “The Empty Chair at the Strategic Table by Dr. Michael R. Blaschke

Enterprise Architecture needs a seat at the table where business strategy and AI investment decisions are made. But that seat cannot simply be claimed because of an architect's title or technical experience. It must be earned through meaningful business relationships, the quality of questions we ask, the perspectives we bring, and the value we create.

Some of the Key takeaways included:

  • Start with WHY before HOW: Understand the business problem and desired outcome before recommending a technology solution.

  • Think and communicate like an executive: Connect architecture decisions to business priorities, value, and long-term direction.

  • Design for enterprise capabilities: Look beyond individual applications and solutions to the capabilities the organization needs to build.

  • Build relationships across the business: Engage business leaders and C-suite stakeholders early rather than waiting for technology decisions to be made.

  • Exercise judgment in AI adoption: Understand where AI can create meaningful value — and recognize when a different approach may be more appropriate.

One thought from the day particularly resonated: “We don't just move data; we move human possibilities.” It was a reminder that architecture is ultimately about enabling people, improving decisions, and creating opportunities through technology.

From AI Possibilities to Agentic AI Value Realization

Program moved the conversation from the promise of AI to the practical realities of Agentic AI. The focus was on trusted enterprise context, realizing business value from AI agents, and maintaining human responsibility as organizations move toward greater autonomy.

Some of the survey findings highlighted a significant gap between AI experimentation and enterprise-wide value realization. Organizations may be exploring AI agents, but scaling them requires much more than technology implementation. It requires clear business objectives, trusted data, enterprise context, governance, accountability, and measurable outcomes.

Another finding was equally important: only 9% of respondents said Enterprise Architecture leads AI decisions in their organizations, while 40% indicated that EA is informed after decisions have been made or is not involved but is still expected to deliver.

This reinforces the importance of Enterprise Architects becoming active participants in AI strategy and investment decisions — not simply implementation partners brought in after the direction has already been established.

Some of the key takeaways from the sessions were:

  • Define business value upfront: Every AI initiative should have a clear purpose and measurable business KPIs.

  • Build trusted enterprise context: AI agents need reliable data, business context, and organizational knowledge to deliver meaningful results.

  • Bring Enterprise Architecture into AI decisions early: Architects should help shape the strategy, operating model, integration, and governance of AI initiatives.

  • Measure the work AI creates, not just the work it saves: Evaluate the broader impact of AI on business processes, productivity, and new opportunities.

  • Keep human judgment and accountability central: As autonomy increases, responsible oversight and decision-making become even more important.

  • Explore practical AI opportunities for architects: Documentation, design, discovery, and other architecture activities can benefit from AI-enabled productivity.

 

My Reflections – From Architecting Technology to Shaping the AI-Driven Enterprise

Having participated in the Multidimensional Architect Program since its inception in 2024, I see a clear progression in both the program and the expectations placed on Enterprise Architects.

The 2026 discussions made me reflect on how our profession is evolving. For years, architects have focused on designing technology landscapes, defining integration strategies, establishing governance, and delivering complex transformation programs. Those responsibilities remain important, but the emergence of AI and autonomous agents is expanding the scope of our contribution.

The architect of tomorrow must be able to connect business strategy, enterprise architecture, trusted data, AI capabilities, and human judgment. We need to understand not only how AI works, but where it creates value, how it fits into the enterprise operating model, how it can be governed responsibly, and how its outcomes can be measured.

For me, the biggest shift is this: we must move from architecting solutions for the business to helping the business reimagine what is possible with AI.

This also connects closely with my own professional journey — from leading complex SAP transformations and S/4HANA upgrade programs to exploring AI-driven architecture, automation, and intelligent operations. The program further strengthened my interest in applying AI not just as another technology layer, but as an enabler of better decisions, more efficient operations, and new business capabilities.

Three Years of Evolution – One Changing Profession

Looking back at the three editions, I see more than the evolution of a learning program. I see a reflection of how the Enterprise Architect role itself is changing.

Year       Focus                                                                     The shift

2024Rethinking the ArchitectFrom technology expertise to a broader mindset
2025Becoming MultidimensionalFrom technical leadership to business, people, and strategic influence
2026Architecting the Autonomous EnterpriseFrom AI awareness to AI strategy, agentic capabilities, and measurable business value

Each year built on the previous one. The journey started with transforming how we think, expanded into how we lead and influence, and now challenges us to shape the future of AI-driven enterprises.

The Road Ahead – What Will Define the Enterprise Architect of Tomorrow?

As AI continues to evolve, I believe the Enterprise Architect will increasingly become a bridge between business strategy, technology innovation, and human potential.

The architects who will make the greatest impact are those who can:

  • Think strategically and understand business value.

  • Combine deep technology expertise with AI fluency.

  • Design enterprise-wide capabilities rather than isolated solutions.

  • Translate complexity into clear stories and actionable roadmaps.

  • Champion trusted, responsible, and governed AI adoption.

  • Influence decisions, inspire people, and lead organizational change.

  • Continuously learn, unlearn, relearn, and share knowledge with the community.

My journey through the SAP Multidimensional Architect Program over these three years has been both inspiring and motivating. It has encouraged me to challenge my own perspectives, broaden my professional horizons, share my experiences through writing, and continuously explore how emerging technologies can create meaningful impact.

I am grateful to the SAP Institute for Product and Engineering, the program organizers, speakers, fellow architects, and the wider Enterprise Architecture community for creating an environment where learning goes beyond presentations — through conversations, shared experiences, new perspectives, and lasting connections.

 

Personal Achievements & Highlights – When Learning Turned into a Proud Moment

Beyond the incredible learning, insights, and inspiration I gained throughout the three-day journey, the most memorable moment was saved for the very end truly the icing on the cake!

A special and heartfelt appreciation to Paul Kurchina for taking the opportunity to recognize and promote my book, “SAP S/4HANA Upgrades & Updates: Mastering Zero Downtime Option,” and for sharing its relevance with the architect community. Seeing my work acknowledged and highlighted in such a forum was both humbling and immensely rewarding. It was particularly meaningful because the book represents years of hands-on experience, practical learnings, and a personal commitment to sharing knowledge with the broader SAP ecosystem.

What made the moment even more special was the connection highlighted between the book's subject and the value our SAP MaxAttention team can bring to customers through our expertise in Zero Downtime Option (ZDO) and SAP S/4HANA upgrade approaches, we can help customers address one of their biggest transformation concerns minimizing business downtime while navigating complex upgrades and conversions. It was a great opportunity to reinforce how our team's experience, guidance, and technical capabilities can help customers plan and execute their transformation journeys with reduced downtime and greater confidence.

For me, this was more than just a book promotion. It was a proud moment where personal knowledge-sharing, professional achievement, and customer value came together. It reinforced my belief that the experience we gain through customer engagements becomes even more meaningful when we document it, share it, and use it to help others succeed.

I couldn't have asked for a more fulfilling way to conclude this year's program — taking away new perspectives, strengthening connections, and seeing my own contribution create visibility and potential value for the wider SAP community.

My biggest takeaway from these three years is simple:

  • 2024 taught us to think differently. 2025 inspired us to become multidimensional. 2026 challenged us to architect and think differently in AI world.
  • The future Enterprise Architect will not simply design the enterprise of today. They will help shape the autonomous, intelligent, and human-centered enterprise of tomorrow.

And that, to me, is the true meaning of being a Multidimensional Architect.

entry.title: Every Phase. Every Tool. Every Decision. How SAP Has Woven AI Into Transformation
entry.content:
Having worked closely on transformation Projects, one shift stands out above everything else right now — and it's not a new tool or a new methodology. It's the intelligence that's been woven into the toolchain itself. Teams are spending less time on the work that slows projects down, and more time on the decisions that actually move them forward. Here's what's driving that change.

The Toolchain Didn't Change. Its Intelligence Did.

The core of SAP's integrated toolchain — Signavio, LeanIX, Cloud ALM, Tricentis, Syniti, WalkMe — remains intact. What's changed is what runs inside it. AI, agents, and assistants are now embedded across every tool and every phase. The result isn't a new toolchain. It's the same toolchain, made capable of thinking.

This is why SAP has renamed it the Agent-Led Toolchain — not as branding, but as an accurate description of how it now works.

Two Layers of Intelligence Working in Tandem

At the heart of the evolution are two distinct AI layers:

Joule Assistants sit at the experience layer. Think of them as an experienced project manager — role-aware, context-aware, and able to understand what a Finance Manager, Project Lead, or IT Consultant actually needs. They don't act directly. They coordinate, routing the right agents, tools, and skills to fulfil a complex task.

Joule Agents sit at the execution layer. These are the specialists. Autonomous, task-specific, and deeply embedded in SAP's business processes — S/4HANA, SuccessFactors, Ariba — they can independently plan and execute multi-step workflows without constant human approval. Multiple agents can collaborate across functions simultaneously.

Together, they create a system where human intent gets translated into executed outcomes — with minimal friction in between.

Where AI Lives Across the Toolchain

SAP LeanIX — Architecture, Built Automatically The AI-Assisted Inventory Builder reads diagrams and images to create architecture fact sheets without manual input. The Enterprise Architecture Assistant enriches the inventory, recommends models, and generates reports. What previously took weeks of discovery is largely automated from day one.

SAP Signavio — Processes Understood in Plain Language The Process Consulting Agent lets teams analyse and consult on business processes through natural language. Text to Insights and Text to Widget turn conversational questions into process analytics instantly — no analyst required to build the query.

SAP Cloud ALM — AI-Guided Lifecycle Management SAP Cloud ALM anchors project and quality management across the transformation. With AI embedded across the wider toolchain, teams benefit from intelligent guidance at every phase — keeping scope, quality gates, and the success plan on track.

Tricentis — Testing That Repairs Itself The self-healing test automation adapts when application interfaces change, removing the need for manual script maintenance after every sprint. The testing copilot supports test asset creation, cutting the time to build a solid test library.

Syniti — Data Migration Without the Guesswork Syniti's AI handles the heavy lifting in data matching and migration, ensuring data integrity before it reaches production. — catching issues long before they reach production. The riskiest part of any project becomes structured and auditable.

WalkMe — Adoption Ready Before Go-Live AI Authoring generates in-application guidance from natural-language input. Learning Arc creates training content directly from SOPs and reference materials. AI Insights surfaces workflow friction from real user behaviour — so teams fix problems before they become support tickets. The Joule Action Bar extends this intelligence across SAP and non-SAP applications.

What This Unlocks for Project Implementation

Discovery in days, not weeks. LeanIX auto-detects SAP applications and components, building an accurate architecture picture from the start — without a manual inventory sprint.

Process design that keeps pace with the project. Signavio's AI iterates on process analysis in hours. Workshops still matter, but the baseline arrives faster and smarter.

No more design-to-delivery drift. AI-maintained alignment between Signavio and LeanIX means process decisions stay connected to architecture decisions throughout the build. Scope ambiguity — one of the biggest drivers of project overruns — gets structurally reduced.

Testing that doesn't become the bottleneck. Every sprint changes something. Self-healing tests adapt automatically. Regression cycles shrink. Release velocity holds.

Data migration as a managed risk, not a crisis. Syniti's AI validates data quality continuously. By go-live, there are no surprises — because issues were caught and resolved in the migration pipeline, not in production.

Users ready on day one. WalkMe generates contextual guidance from existing documentation and delivers it inside the application, precisely when users need it. Post-go-live adoption lag — historically one of the most expensive outcomes of any project — becomes a solved problem.

And it doesn't stop at go-live. The same toolchain that drove implementation stays active afterwards. The agents and assistants don't switch off — they shift from transformation mode to continuous improvement mode. What was built to deliver becomes the foundation for an organisation that keeps optimising itself.

AI hasn't improved individual tools at the margin. It has changed the nature of what the toolchain can do — turning a connected set of products into a system that understands context, executes autonomously, and learns continuously.

entry.title: Joule Agents on SAP Cloud ERP Private: What Really Happens When You Try to Activate One
entry.content:
There are three ways to get a Joule agent working on SAP Cloud ERP Private. Before any of them matters, there is one check that decides whether a single one of them is open to you.

You have AI Units on the contract. Business Data Cloud is provisioned. Finance has an approved use case and a sponsor.

Someone asks you the obvious question: "We have S/4HANA, Business Data Cloud and AI Units. So which agents do we build in S/4, and which ones on BDC?"

It is a good question from a well prepared team, and it contains a category error. Neither S/4HANA nor Business Data Cloud is a place where agents are built. But that is not the reason the project stalls. You open the agent's Discovery Center page, and the minimum release is SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS01, restricted to Early Adopter Care. Production is on 2023. Today the answer is not one platform or the other. It is none of the three paths, and nobody in the conversation had mentioned it.

There is also something that has to be settled before any of that, and it is not one of the three paths.

It is the release. On SAP Cloud ERP Private the minimum release differs per agent. The Accounting Accruals Agent used in this example requires S/4HANA 2025 FPS01, and at the time of writing it is available only to customers enrolled in Early Adopter Care. Check each agent against SAP Note 3789370 rather than assuming a common floor.

Once a landscape is above that line, two things decide which path applies: what the thing has to produce when it finishes, and how far it has to reach to produce it. Answer those and the path picks itself.

So this post does two things. It establishes where to check that first, and then it walks the three paths that the choice is actually between, with one finance process carried along each of them.

Reach drawn as radius. Each path stops at a boundary, and that boundary is the reason the next one exists.

Three words worth getting right

Most of the confusion in these conversations is vocabulary, not architecture.

Term

What it actually is

Joule Assistant

The orchestrator. It takes the user's intent, plans the work, picks which agents to invoke, sequences them, and assembles the answer. It decides the what and the when.

Joule Agent

A task executor with a narrow, pre-defined scope. It decides how to accomplish its objective inside that scope. It does not control the wider flow.

Agent Extension

A Joule Studio solution type. SAP's own description: custom skills, instructions or data fields added to existing SAP agents.

The last one is the one most people have never heard of, and it is the one that resolves the majority of these conversations.

And a second set, because SAP renamed the products

In 2025 SAP renamed its cloud ERP offerings, and the rename is still visible in some places and not others. The old and new names both circulate.

  • SAP Cloud ERP was S/4HANA Cloud, public edition. Multi-tenant, SAP schedules the upgrades, no deferral, standard code cannot be modified. The journey is SAP GROW.
  • SAP Cloud ERP Private was S/4HANA Cloud, private edition. Single tenant, the customer schedules upgrades and can defer them, full ABAP development. The journey is RISE with SAP.
  • SAP HANA Cloud is not ERP at all. It is a managed database service on BTP, and it is what Datasphere and Business Data Cloud sit on. Every S/4HANA system uses a HANA database internally, but that is not the product. A customer who says "we are on HANA Cloud" has told you about their data platform and nothing about their ERP.

That confusion matters more than it looks. Before you can compare paths you need to know which ERP edition the customer runs, because the edition decides which agents exist for them at all. The same agent can be available on one edition and absent on the other, so an answer about their data platform does not answer the question you asked.

Path one: activate what SAP already delivers

The test for this path is simple. Does SAP's encoded logic already match how the customer works? If it does, nothing gets built.

Take the SAP Accounting Accruals Agent, reached through the Financial Closing Assistant, as the worked example. Here is what actually happens.

An accountant asks in Joule to prepare accruals for a period and company code. The Assistant routes the intent to the agent. The agent reads two things: the company's own accrual policy handbook, uploaded as a document, and transaction data in the Universal Journal, which includes open purchase orders, goods receipts without an invoice, prepayments and the GR/IR clearing account, plus what is already posted for the period so it does not duplicate. It applies the policy rules against a configured materiality threshold, and produces journal entry proposals, each one carrying a plain-language rationale naming the transactions and the rule it applied.

Those proposals land in the Manage Accrual Proposals Fiori app, where a GL accountant accepts, modifies or rejects each one and posts the accepted entries.

The agent does not post. That is the product, not a configuration choice. That single fact answers most of what a finance team wants to know before it lets an agent near the ledger.

Two things about this flow that surprise people

First, a delivered agent is reading the organisation's own document. If you assume that an SAP-delivered agent cannot read your own documents, you will start building a custom agent when uploading a file would have been enough. That single assumption is the most common reason teams reach for Build when Activate would have worked.

The handbook has real constraints worth knowing before you promise anything. It is uploaded by asking Joule for it from the Manage Accrual Proposals app. It must be a PDF, it supports a maximum of five expense categories before proposal generation times out, and it must name company codes, expense categories and calculation rules, with everything for a given company code in one document. A new upload overwrites the previous one immediately, with no versioning and no approval workflow, which is worth knowing before a period close depends on it.

Second, the minimum release is per agent, not per product. On SAP Cloud ERP Private the Autonomous Finance agents currently require S/4HANA 2025 FPS01. The SAP Discovery Center pages for the Accounting Accruals Agent and the Receivables and Payables Clearing Agent both state that version, and both list the agent as available only to customers enrolled in an Early Adopter Care programme. SAP Note 3789370 carries the same picture for Private Edition. Check the agent's own page against the system's release rather than relying on a product-level answer.

Activation is not a project. It is three things: switching the agent on, writing the policy document it reads, and training the people who work the review app. You know it worked when the team closes one period with the agent running beside them. If that is all the customer needs, stop here. There is no reason to look at the other two paths.

Path two: extend what SAP delivers

The test here is the one that separates most real conversations from imagined ones. Is this the same output, computed by a different rule?

If the customer's process produces the same thing SAP's agent produces but arrives at it differently, you extend. You do not replace.

Agent Extensions are a named solution type in Joule Studio, alongside Agents, n8n Workflows and Applications. SAP's Architecture Center describes what one consists of in a single line: custom skills, instructions or data fields added to existing SAP agents. Three things, named.

Stay with the accruals example. Suppose the business accrues freight from contracted lane rates held in a custom field on the purchase order, while SAP's logic reads invoice history. And suppose the European company codes work to a different materiality threshold from the US ones. Neither of those is a new process. Both still end in an accrual proposal, reviewed in the
same app and posted to the same ledger. That is the test for Extend rather than Build: the thing the agent produces does not change, only the rule that produces it. Three changes cover it. A custom data field makes the lane rate visible to the calculation.
A custom instruction sets materiality by company code instead of one global number. And a custom skill calls a control the delivered agent does not know about.

What the customer keeps

This is the part most often left out of the comparison.

  • SAP's data reads stay as delivered
  • The output is still an accrual proposal, carrying its reasoning
  • SAP keeps maintaining and upgrading the delivered agent, so the underlying logic stays their responsibility rather than becoming yours. With a custom agent, that maintenance moves to you.
  • SAP keeps maintaining and upgrading the delivered agent, so the underlying logic stays their responsibility rather than becoming yours. With a custom agent, that maintenance moves to you.

That last point matters more than it looks. Extend, and the agent is positioned to inherit SAP's next version. Rebuild the same thing from scratch and it has to be maintained against every release, which is a cost that shows up in year two rather than year one.

Two honest limits

Extensions do not port between editions. SAP's clean core guidance puts it plainly: extensions created for private edition generally require adaptations to be portable to the public cloud, side-by-side extensions on BTP are more likely to be compatible because they decouple the logic from the core, and complete parity is not guaranteed because API availability and scope differ across editions. There is a second, more practical point at the time of writing. Every published extension tutorial targets a Public Edition agent, and I could not find one that extends a Private Edition agent. Whether that reflects what the catalogue actually offers, or only what has been written up so far, I cannot tell from public sources. Worth checking against your own tenant rather than taking from a post.

And the upgrade behaviour is positioning, not a published guarantee. SAP has built extension as the path that respects the release train, and that is the architectural intent. The mechanism itself is not documented, and extension points appear to be declared per agent rather than universally. Worth confirming for the specific agent rather than assuming it holds generally.

Path three: build in Joule Studio

The test for this one: is the output a different thing entirely?

If what the customer wants does not exist as an SAP business object, no delivered agent will ever produce it, because it is not an SAP process. It is this company's question. That is when you build, and it is the only honest reason to.

Stay with finance and the shape is obvious. The accruals agent produces a proposal. Suppose the CFO wants something else: two weeks before close, what the accrual exposure is likely to land at across the whole group, including commitments sitting in a third-party receivables platform that never enters S/4HANA, compared against the same quarter in prior years that the ERP no longer keeps online.

That is not an accrual proposal. It is a briefing with a recommendation. Different object, so neither activate nor extend can reach it.

What a Joule Studio agent is actually made of

An agent is a definition plus a set of tools, not a programme.

The definition carries a name, a description, its expertise and its instructions, and Joule uses that description to decide when to route a request to it. You select a model available through the generative AI hub. Then you add tools. The assignable tool types today are:

  • Joule Skills, single deterministic actions
  • Actions, API calls to SAP or third-party systems
  • Automations, Build Process Automation workflows
  • Document grounding resource groups
  • MCP server tools, reached over BTP destinations
  • Other custom agents, used as subagents
  • Human-in-the-loop confirmation points, so the agent pauses for approval at the decisions that matter

This is where Business Data Cloud genuinely belongs, and notice that it arrived on the third path rather than the first. A question that spans entities, spans years and spans systems is exactly what the data layer exists for, and almost nothing before this point needed it.

One limit people assume away

A custom agent can use other custom agents as subagents. It cannot call an SAP-delivered agent. The current interoperability model works inbound: a third-party or custom agent can invoke a delivered Joule Agent through the Agent Gateway. The reverse, a Joule Studio agent calling a delivered SAP agent, is a later iteration, and Joule orchestrating mixed chains of delivered and custom agents is planned rather than shipped.

So a design that assumes a new agent will delegate to the Accruals Agent needs checking before it reaches a whiteboard.

One more thing worth stating plainly, because it is the first question anyone responsible for the ledger will ask: a custom agent runs in the calling user's security context. SAP's own product page puts it directly, saying that all agent traffic flows through the agent gateway, so agents can only execute what the end user has permission to do directly. An agent is not a route around access control.

 

One front door, three places the work lands, and only the third reaching outside the ERP.

The boundary nobody checks

Everything above is about choosing a path. This section is about whether the customer's use case is reachable from any of them, and it is the part most often skipped.

An agent activation is scoped to one backend and one client.

The mechanism is the skills mapping. Each agent has pre-defined Joule Skills that map to specific intended back ends, and only back ends with official, delivered skills are eligible targets for that agent's execution. Routing follows the step ownership defined in the delivered process. There is no mechanism for a single active agent to query or route across multiple clients or backend systems within one conversation turn.

Joule can surface agents from different connected systems in the same interface, which is why this is easy to miss. But each agent still executes against the backend its skills were mapped to, and SAP's product page states the permission boundary directly: all agent traffic flows through the agent gateway, so agents can only execute what the end user has permission to do directly.

How many systems one Joule instance can front is a separate question, and SAP's documentation currently disagrees with itself about it. The constraints pages say a Joule instance links to a single S/4HANA system. The Q2 2026 release notes and the Joule Feature Summary Document say Joule supports connecting multiple Private Edition and Public Edition systems within one formation. Until those reconcile it is not a number worth quoting. What holds either way is the agent-level constraint above: whatever Joule can front, an individual agent still executes against one backend.

Why this decides so many conversations

Consider a landscape with one production client live today and further regional clients built and tested but not yet promoted. Everything works. The agent sits in the live client, reads what it needs, proposes, a person posts.

Now the regional waves land. Each client that goes live needs its own activation, and each of those agents executes against its own client. Joule can front all of them, so a user still asks one question and is routed to the right system. What no single agent does is reason across all five in one turn.

One activation per client. Joule fronts all of them; no single agent reasons across them.

So the question that genuinely spans the clients is not answered by any delivered agent, and it is not answered by an extension either, because extending changes the rule and not the reach. It is answerable where those clients converge, which is the data layer. That is the honest case for Business Data Cloud, and it is a better case than the one usually made for it, because it comes from a constraint rather than from a product sheet.

This belongs alongside the release check, before the catalogue is opened at all. A use case whose data sits in another client, another instance, or in a legacy ERP that only replicates financial documents in, is not reachable from the activate path however many AI Units are already paid for.

What this looks like in a real landscape

A worked example makes this concrete. What follows is a real customer environment with the identifying detail stripped out. Nothing in it is unusual, and that is exactly why it is worth walking through.

They run Cloud ERP Private on release 2023, with a second landscape on release 2025 being built in parallel. Production carries one business client. Several further clients exist in quality and development, configured and tested, waiting on the regional rollout. Central Finance is live, replicating financial documents in from legacy ERP systems still running finance in some parts of the world.

Four things follow from that. The first three are checkable; the fourth is a question I could not resolve.

None of the three paths is open to them yet. The finance agents need 2025 FPS01 and Early Adopter Care enrolment, and the business runs on 2023. The second landscape is where the paths become available, so the first move is finishing that migration, not choosing between agents.

This limit is not theoretical, and it already has a date. With one production client today, one activation covers the whole business and nobody runs into a boundary. When the regional clients go live, each one needs its own agent, and no single agent can answer a question that spans them. That is the moment Build becomes the honest answer, and the go-live date for those clients is already in somebody's plan.

Central Finance changes what the agent can see. The accruals agent reads open purchase orders, goods receipts without an invoice, and the GR/IR clearing account. Central Finance replicates financial and controlling postings plus a defined subset of logistics through the accounting view of logistics. That is an accounting view, not the logistics document chain. Whether it satisfies what the agent's logic expects is a real question, and I have not seen it answered publicly. The practical consequence is that processes posted natively in the live client are reachable, and regions still running in a legacy ERP are not.

Almost the whole surrounding stack is already there. Cloud Identity Services, Build Work Zone, the connectivity and destination services, Integration Suite and the Business AI Platform are all live in the production landscape, as are Business Data Cloud and Datasphere. When the release does arrive, this is a configuration exercise rather than a procurement one, which is worth establishing on any landscape early.

Four questions, in order

These work on any process, not only finance, and they take about five minutes.

Which release is it on, and is the agent available there?

The product, the release and the feature pack, then that agent's own Discovery Center page. On Cloud ERP Private the finance agents need 2025 FPS01 and Early Adopter Care enrolment. Below that line there is no path to choose yet, and every question after this one is academic.

What does it produce, and where is the data?

A posted document, a cleared item, a proposal for review, or a briefing. If the output is the same business object SAP's agent already produces, the answer is path one or two. A different object means path three. Then: which client holds the data it needs, because one agent reads one backend and one client.

Is the gap the process, or the rule?

Does SAP's agent do the right job the wrong way, or the wrong job entirely? Right job, wrong way is an extension, and it is usually a few fields and an instruction. Wrong job entirely is the only honest reason to build. This is the question most often skipped, and skipping it is how a few fields and an instruction turn into a project.

Does the non-SAP system supply data, or make decisions?

A non-SAP system is either a source you read from or a system that acts on its own. Reading its data is a connection you configure, which keeps you on the Build path with a shape you can scope and price. Having that system make decisions on your behalf is a different problem, and not all of it is available today. Answering this question tells you whether Build means a data connection you can commit to now, or something you should not promise yet.

Most of these conversations start at Build, because that is the conversation the market has trained everyone to have. Starting at the release and working down is the shorter route to something that actually ships.

* Product behaviour changes quickly here. Everything above is current as of late October 2026, and the per-agent release floors in particular are worth re-checking rather than quoting from a post.

To transfer a custom field from Purchase Requisition (EBAN) to Purchase Order (EKPO) during creation or change via ME21N / ME22N, follow standard enhancement architecture:

  1. Data Dictionary Preparation:

  • Ensure the custom field (e.g., ZZFIELD) exists in the CI_EBANDB include (for table EBAN) and CI_EKPODB include (for table EKPO).

  • Verify field technical attributes (Data Element / Domain) match identically in both tables.

  1. Best Practice Enhancement: BAdI Implementation The standard and recommended approach in ECC and S/4HANA is using the BAdI ME_PROCESS_PO_CUST:

  • Implement BAdI ME_PROCESS_PO_CUST via transaction SE19.

  • Use method PROCESS_ITEM: a. Get the current PO item data using method im_item->get_data( ). b. Check if a reference Purchase Requisition exists by validating BANFN and BNFPO. c. If BANFN is populated, select the custom value from EBAN:

SELECT SINGLE zzfield
FROM eban
INTO @DATA(lv_zzfield)
WHERE banfn = @LS_mepoitem-banfn
AND bnfpo = @LS_mepoitem-bnfpo.

d. Populate the custom field into your PO item structure:
ls_mepoitem-zzfield = lv_zzfield.
e. Update the item back to the document memory using:
im_item->set_data( ls_mepoitem ).

  1. Alternative (Classic Customer-Exit): If using classic enhancement exits:

  • Use Enhancement MM06E005 (Component: EXIT_SAPMM06E_016 or EXIT_SAPMM06E_018 for Item data transfer).

  • Ensure custom subscreen fields are mapped via Function Group XM06.

Using ME_PROCESS_PO_CUST method PROCESS_ITEM remains the cleaner, fully S/4HANA-compatible approach.

entry.title: The Hidden Security Habit Every SAP BTP Admin Must Master: Service Key Rotation
entry.content:
Introduction: the credential nobody owns

A service key is usually created in thirty seconds, pasted into a .env file or a CI variable or Destination or any 3rd Party applications, and then forgotten for years. That is exactly why it becomes one of the most dangerous objects in your SAP BTP landscape.

If you integrate anything with BTP from outside the platform (a local development machine, an on-premise system, a GitHub Actions pipeline, a low-code tool such as n8n), you almost certainly rely on service keys. They give you a client ID and secret, or a certificate, that unlocks a service instance: XSUAA, Destination, Object Store, Cloud Logging, SAP AI Core and many more.

This blogpost explains what service keys really are, why you must rotate them, and how to do it without downtime, using the cf CLI, the btp CLI and a small automation pattern you can drop into a pipeline.

What a service key is (and is not)

A service key is a set of credentials generated on demand for an existing service instance. It is meant for clients that live outside the platform. Credentials meant for an application running inside Cloud Foundry or Kyma are called service bindings, and they reach the app through VCAP_SERVICES or a Kubernetes secret. The mechanics are the same, which is why this post applies to both.

For an XSUAA instance, a key typically contains the following fields:

  • clientid and clientsecret: the OAuth 2.0 client credentials
  • url and uaadomain: the token endpoint host
  • xsappname, identityzone, tenantid: identifiers of the application and subaccount
  • verificationkey: the public key used to validate issued JWTs

Whoever holds the clientid and clientsecret can request tokens with the scopes of the service instance, from anywhere on the internet. There is no IP restriction and no user attached. The key is the identity.

Credential types

Many BTP services let you choose how a key authenticates. The choice decides how painful rotation will be.

Credential type

What you get

Rotation effort

Typical risk

Client secret (default, binding-secret)

clientid + clientsecret

Create a new key, replace the secret everywhere

A leaked string works until you delete the key

X.509 certificate

Client certificate and private key (mTLS)

Keys expire by design; re-issue before expiry

Needs the private key, not just a string

Instance secret

One secret shared by the instance

Rotation touches every consumer at once

Large blast radius

For X.509 on XSUAA you request the type when creating the key, with a short validity:

cf create-service-key my-xsuaa key-x509 -c '{
  "credential-type": "x509",
  "x509": { "key-length": 2048, "validity": 7, "validity-type": "DAYS" }
}'

Supported parameters differ per service, so check the documentation of the service you use on SAP Help Portal .

Why rotation is needed

A service key never expires on its own (unless you chose X.509 with a validity). Every day it exists, the chance that it has leaked grows, and you never learn about the leak until it is abused. Rotation puts a ceiling on that exposure.

  • Leaks are silent. Keys end up in shell history, screenshots, support tickets, Postman collections, Git commits and CI logs. A leaked key looks identical to a legitimate one in the logs.
  • People and projects leave. The developer who created a key for a proof of concept may have left the company. Rotation, combined with an inventory, forces someone to claim every key or let it die.
  • Blast radius. A key carries the scopes of the whole instance. Short-lived or frequently replaced keys limit how long an attacker can use what they stole.
  • Compliance. Frameworks such as ISO 27001, SOC 2 and internal security policies commonly require periodic credential rotation and evidence that it happens.
  • Proof that you can do it. The worst time to learn that rotating a credential breaks three undocumented consumers is during an incident. A routine rotation is a fire drill you run on your own schedule.

What it buys you in an incident

If rotation is a routine, a suspected leak becomes a normal operation: create a new key, move consumers over, delete the old key. If it is not a routine, you face a decision between a possible breach and a possible outage, usually at night.

Deleting a key revokes its client secret at the service, so a rotation also invalidates any copy someone made earlier. Tokens that were already issued stay valid until they expire, which is why short token lifetimes matter as well.

The zero-downtime pattern: overlap, switch, retire

The key point is that a service instance can have several keys at the same time. You never edit a key in place. You add a second one next to the first, and you retire the first only after every consumer has moved.

  1. Inventory. List the existing keys and find out who uses each one.
  2. Create a new key with a versioned or dated name, for example ci-2026-10.
  3. Distribute the new credentials to your secret store or CI system.
  4. Switch the consumers: redeploy, restart or let them reload the secret.
  5. Verify that the consumers obtain tokens with the new key and that errors stay flat.
  6. Wait a grace period, so that slow consumers (nightly jobs, a colleague's laptop) fail loudly rather than silently.
  7. Delete the old key. This is the step that actually closes the leak.

Two habits make this reliable. First, name keys with a purpose and a date (n8n-prod-2026-10), so age and owner are visible in a listing. Second, give each consumer its own key. If five systems share one key, you can rotate it only by switching five systems on the same day, and you cannot tell which of them used it last.

Hands-on: rotating a key with the CLI

Cloud Foundry (cf CLI)

Start with an inventory of the keys on the instance:

cf service-keys my-xsuaa

Create the replacement key and read its credentials through the API, which is more robust to script than the formatted CLI output:

NEW_KEY="n8n-prod-$(date +%Y-%m)"
cf create-service-key my-xsuaa "$NEW_KEY"

GUID=$(cf service-key my-xsuaa "$NEW_KEY" --guid)
cf curl "/v3/service_credential_bindings/$GUID/details" | jq '.credentials'

After the consumers have switched and the grace period is over, remove the old key:

cf delete-service-key my-xsuaa n8n-prod-2026-09 -f

For service bindings used by apps, the equivalent is to create a new binding and restart the app so it reads the new VCAP_SERVICES. A rolling restart avoids downtime:

cf restart my-app --strategy rolling

Other environments (btp CLI and Service Manager)

In Kyma or any non-Cloud-Foundry environment, keys are called bindings and are managed through Service Manager. The btp CLI exposes them: btp CLI

btp list services/binding
btp create services/binding --name ci-2026-10 --service-instance my-xsuaa
btp delete services/binding --name ci-2026-09 --confirm

In Kyma, the equivalent is a ServiceBinding resource that writes the credentials to a Kubernetes secret. Creating a second ServiceBinding and pointing the workload at the new secret follows the same overlap pattern. Command flags change between CLI versions, so confirm them with btp help before you script anything.

Automating rotation and storing the result

Manual rotation works once. A scheduled job works every time. The script below creates a fresh key, hands the credentials to your secret store, and deletes keys older than a grace period. It is a starting point, not a drop-in product: adapt the secret-store call and test it on a non-production instance first.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

INSTANCE="$1"            # service instance name
PREFIX="$2"              # key name prefix, e.g. n8n-prod
GRACE_DAYS="${3:-14}"    # how long old keys stay alive

NEW_KEY="${PREFIX}-$(date +%Y%m%d)"
cf create-service-key "$INSTANCE" "$NEW_KEY"

GUID=$(cf service-key "$INSTANCE" "$NEW_KEY" --guid)
CREDS=$(cf curl "/v3/service_credential_bindings/$GUID/details" | jq -c '.credentials')

# 1. Push to your secret store (never echo or log $CREDS)
#    e.g. vault kv put secret/btp/$PREFIX value="$CREDS"

# 2. Retire old keys of this prefix beyond the grace period
INST_GUID=$(cf service "$INSTANCE" --guid)
CUTOFF=$(date -u -d "-${GRACE_DAYS} days" +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)

cf curl "/v3/service_credential_bindings?type=key&service_instance_guids=${INST_GUID}" \
  | jq -r --arg p "$PREFIX" --arg c "$CUTOFF" --arg n "$NEW_KEY" \
    '.resources[] | select((.name|startswith($p)) and .name != $n and .created_at < $c) | .name' \
  | while read -r OLD; do
      echo "Deleting expired key: $OLD"
      cf delete-service-key "$INSTANCE" "$OLD" -f
    done

Where the new credentials should live

  • A dedicated secret manager. HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or the SAP Credential Store service on BTP. Consumers fetch the secret at start-up or on a refresh interval, so a rotation needs no redeploy.
  • CI/CD secrets. GitHub Actions, GitLab CI or Jenkins credentials, updated by the rotation job through their API.
  • Not in Git, not in images, not in chat. Not even in a private repository, and not as a plain environment variable baked into a container image.

Run the job on a schedule, for example every 60 or 90 days, and make the grace period shorter than the interval. Alert when a rotation fails, because a silent failure is worse than no automation: it creates the false impression that the problem is handled.

The cleanest long-term step is to remove the shared secret entirely. Where the service supports it, prefer X.509 credentials with a short validity, or an identity federation flow such as OIDC trust between your CI provider and BTP, so that no long-lived secret exists to rotate.

Pitfalls, checklist and conclusion

Common pitfalls

  • Deleting before switching. Remove the old key only after you have seen the new one working in production.
  • Forgotten consumers. Cron jobs, notebooks and a colleague's local default-env.json break after the delete. Use the grace period and watch authentication failures.
  • One key for everything. It makes rotation a coordinated big-bang change and hides who uses what.
  • Cached tokens and clients. Applications that read the secret once at start-up need a restart, or a reload mechanism, to pick up the new value.
  • Rotating the key but not the access around it. A new key with the same wide scopes only shortens the exposure. Combine rotation with least-privilege scopes and role collections.
  • No monitoring. Check the audit logs and authentication errors after each rotation; SAP Audit Log service records management operations on service instances.

Checklist

  • Every service key has an owner, a purpose and a date in its name
  • One key per consumer, no shared keys
  • Rotation interval defined (for example 90 days) and automated
  • Credentials live in a secret manager, not in code or images
  • Old keys are deleted after a fixed grace period
  • Failures of the rotation job raise an alert
  • Short-lived X.509 or federated identity used wherever the service supports it

Conclusion

Service key rotation is cheap insurance. It limits how long a leaked credential is useful, it forces you to know who depends on what, and it turns an emergency into a routine. Create the new key beside the old one, move the consumers, verify, wait, delete. Put that on a schedule and the quiet backbone of your BTP integrations stops being its quietest risk.
